newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua ex-contras kidnap gov't peace commission.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua ex-contras kidnap gov't peace commission.

text.p: Former contra rebels have kidnapped eight members of a government peace commission sent to oversee their surrender, a Nicaraguan army spokesman said on Tuesday.

The rebels, part of the Northern Front 3-80 group active in Nicaragua's northern mountains, had planned to disarm and return to civilian life on Tuesday, in accordance with a peace pact signed last month.
Instead, the army said, they took eight members of the government commission hostage at dawn on Tuesday in the village of Kuskawaas, about 150 miles (250 km) north of the capital Managua.
"It is totally confirmed, eight people have been kidnapped by the Northern Front 3-80," army spokesman Milton Sandoval told Reuters.
Lt. Col. Julio Cesar Aviles, the regional chief of the northern province of Matagalpa, also confirmed the kidnapping to official Radio Nicaragua.

Sandoval had earlier said that a churchman, Gustavo Parajon, had also been abducted but the Defence Ministry denied this, saying the kidnapped man was Armando Parajon and was their head of human rights.

But Sergio Caramagna, the director of the Organisation of American States (OAS) mission to assist the peace process, denied that there had been abductions. "We have just talked to them by radio and no one is in danger," he said.

The army insisted, saying that Armando Parajon, the Defence Ministry's director of Human Rights, was among those seized. The Defence Ministry spoke only of "confusion" and said it would explain exactly what happened at a news conference later on Tuesday. Nicaragua's government recently separated the army from the Defence Ministry.

Army officials said the contra rebel group that carried out the kidnapping was led by Jose Vicente Blandon, alias "El Cadejo." Unconfirmed radio reports said the group wanted one of its jailed colleagues to be freed.

The contra rebels, who were heavily backed by then-U.S. President Ronald Reagan, waged war during the 1980s on the revolutionary Sandinista government of Nicaragua. Although Nicaragua is now on its second elected non-Sandinista president, some of the former contra groups remain active in the mountainous north.
Under the terms of the May 30 agreement, the roughly 700 remaining contras were to disband by the middle of July.
